messages.content: 关于论文《Mapping Languages and Demographics with Georeferenced Corpora》，Do they authors offer a hypothesis for why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country?

claims.text: The paper reports that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.

The paper's third important finding is that, given available ground-truth language-use data, there remain countries where the corpora do not represent all languages produced by local populations, and in this case Twitter has fewer missing languages.
The paper states that Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania.
The paper notes that English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so any country predominantly using these two languages will have a good representation by default.
The paper observes that relying on Twitter alone would indicate more diverse language-speaking populations in countries such as the US, Canada, South Africa, France, India, and Australia.

For Russia's false positive rate, the paper says more research is needed to distinguish between immigration, tourism, and business as alternate sources of false positive languages in digital datasets.

The paper hypothesizes that Twitter as a platform represents wealthier populations than general web-crawled data, based on Twitter matching populations better when weighted by GDP and worse when weighted by internet-usage statistics.
An alternate interpretation offered is that the Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have wealthier populations.

The paper's first important finding is that Twitter and web-crawled data diverge significantly in representing the world's population, reflecting that data drawn from Twitter and web pages likely represent people from different places.
